item.title: Bayesian assessment of antarctic grounding line positions with sentinel-1 data and empirical priors
item.dc:creator: Michael Engel, Sindhu Ramanath Tarekere, Lukas Krieger, Jan Wuite, Dana Floricioiu, Marco Körner
item.description:
Remote Sensing of Environment — matched: ice shelf, grounding line, Antarctic, mass loss, sea level, sea-level rise, Bayesian, remote sensing
Bayesian updating provides a powerful route for quantifying uncertainty in geophysical inverse problems, such as the delineation of Antarctic grounding lines (GLs), which demarcate grounded from floating ice. GLs are required to calculate ice mass loss and consequently sea-level rise. However, most existing remote sensing based GL datasets lack spatially resolved positional uncertainty estimates. Hence, we developed an application agnostic Bayesian framework on top of the cross entropy based importance sampling for Bayesian updating (CEBU) algorithm to infer GLs from Sentinel-1 SAR range offsets over the Larsen C Ice Shelf by inverting a simple 1D elastic beam model. We explicitly propagate observational uncertainties through the likelihood and extend CEBU to incorporate empirical ice thickness information as a non-parametric prior. To diagnose convergence and parameter prioritization, we introduce the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance, tracking information flow and enabling identification of non-informative updates. We further developed a data extraction approach that produces spatially dense quasi-1D profiles from 2D range offsets. The resulting GL estimates include full posterior probability density functions which were filtered based on thresholds derived using CEBU metrics. Because range offsets are less affected by interferometric decorrelation, the GLs are spatially and temporally dense. The most probable GL positions have mean and median distances of 361 m and 287 m from the 2019 manually delineated Sentinel-1 DInSAR lines. Our data extraction method also yielded more physically plausible posteriors in shear margin regions than the established flowline-based paradigm. The expert knowledge of ice thicknesses was propagated to other weakly constrained model parameters. This framework enables future development, including model evidence-based comparison of physical formulations, data extraction methods, applications to other ice shelves with challenging tidal or decorrelation conditions, and integration with more comprehensive rheological models. Together, these results highlight the potential of our Bayesian updating framework for a wide variety of large scale geophysical inverse problems.

item.title: All-Weather Antarctic Ice Surface Temperature Retrieval from AMSR2 Using Machine Learning and Spatiotemporal Sampling Strategy
item.dc:creator: Yiran Qin, Quan Zhang, Ninglian Wang, Yuanjun Dang
item.description:
Remote Sensing — matched: ice sheet, Antarctic, Antarctica, polar, machine learning, climate change
Ice surface temperature (IST) is a key variable for characterizing surface energy exchange and climate change over the Antarctic Ice Sheet. Thermal infrared (TIR) IST products provide high spatial resolution observations but suffer from substantial data gaps under cloudy conditions, whereas passive microwave (PMW) observations offer all-weather capability. However, retrieving IST from PMW observations remains challenging due to the complex interactions among microwave emission, snow and ice properties, atmospheric conditions, and surface temperature in polar regions. In this study, an all-weather IST retrieval framework was developed for the Antarctic Ice Sheet by integrating the Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer 2 (AMSR2) brightness temperatures with multi-source environmental variables using machine learning (ML) approaches. MODIS-derived IST estimates were used as reference observations, and a spatiotemporal sampling strategy was proposed to improve the representativeness of training samples under incomplete TIR observations. Three ML models, including Random Forest (RF), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), were developed and evaluated. The results show that all three models successfully reproduced the spatial and seasonal variability of Antarctic IST, with lower uncertainties over the interior ice sheet and relatively higher uncertainties in coastal and ice-shelf margin regions. Among the three models, LightGBM performed most consistently, with RMSEs mainly ranging from 0.50 to 0.60 K relative to MODIS IST. Independent validation against automatic weather station (AWS) observations showed errors broadly comparable to those of MODIS IST, with clear-sky RMSEs of 2.37–5.26 K. The retrieved IST also exhibited consistent daily variations with MODIS observations in 2020, although generally higher temperatures were obtained, reflecting differences in the sensing mechanisms between microwave and TIR. The spatial pattern of the retrieved IST was physically consistent, characterized by the highest temperatures over the Antarctic Peninsula, intermediate temperatures in West Antarctica, and the lowest temperatures in East Antarctica. Overall, the proposed framework improves the spatiotemporal completeness of Antarctic IST observations while maintaining accuracy comparable to MODIS TIR products, supporting more continuous monitoring of Antarctic surface thermal processes and climate variability under all-weather conditions.

item.title: Post-depositional processes affecting water stable isotope records at Little Dome C, Antarctica: new records from two firn cores and virtual firn core modelling
item.dc:creator: Emma Samin, Amaëlle Landais, Elise Fourré, Mathieu Casado, Adrien Ooms, Niels Dutrievoz, … (+5)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: Antarctica, firn
This study presents the water isotope profiles of two firn cores drilled at Little Dome C (LDC) in Antarctica and dated by identifying volcanic events, which enabled us to determine an accumulation rate at LDC of 24 mmwe.yr-1. Comparison of a virtual firn core model with these data allowed us to study the surface processes responsible for isotopic variability in firn. We therefore suggest that future models consider the mixing of the surface layer and re-quantify diffusion.

item.title: Joint Bayesian calibration of frontal ablation and climatic mass balance in global glacier models (PyGEM-OGGM-SERMeQ v1.0)
item.dc:creator: Ruitang Yang, Lizz Ultee, Kristoffer Aalstad, Matvey V. Debolskiy, Regine Hock, Patrick Schmitt, … (+2)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: glacier, calving, Bayesian
We present a new framework to model frontal ablation of marine-terminating glaciers by linking two global glacier models with a simple physics-based calving scheme and Bayesian calibration. Applied to 71 Svalbard glaciers (2000–2019) and projected to 2100, it reproduces seasonal front changes but overestimates ablation due to uncertain geometry and velocity. This efficient approach can improve regional to global simulations.

item.title: Estimating Ocean Heat Content from Satellite Altimetry, Space Gravimetry, and In Situ Observations closes the Earth’s Energy Budget on Interannual to Decadal Time-scales
item.dc:creator: Sébastien Fourest, Benoît Meyssignac, Thomas Duvignacq, Valentin Oncle, Sara Armaut, Sarah L. Connors
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: sea level, satellite altimetry
The ocean stores more than 90% of the excess energy associated with Earth’s radiative imbalance (EEI), making accurate ocean heat content (OHC) estimates essential for closing the global energy budget. We introduce MOHeaCANv6, a new global OHC reconstruction for 2004–2023 that combines satellite altimetry, space gravimetry, and in-situ Argo observations within a unified inverse framework. Satellite-derived thermosteric sea level provides a physically-based prior, locally calibrated to Argo OHC using least squares, followed by objective mapping of residuals to recover unresolved variability. This approach exploits the global coverage and continuity of satellites while retaining Argo’s in-situ accuracy. MOHeaCANv6 provides spatially and temporally consistent OHC estimates for 0–1000m, extended to full depth using satellite constraints on vertically integrated OHC. Cross-validation against withheld Argo profiles indicates local errors generally below 10%(2σ) of the signal. Globally, OHC increases at 9.8±2.1ZJyr −1 (2σ), corresponding to a mean ocean heat uptake (OHU) of 0.81±0.23Wm −2 (2σ) over 2004–2023, with an OHU trend of 0.58±0.4Wm −2 dec −1 (2σ) over 2005–2022. A key result is the close agreement between OHU and an independent estimate derived from CERES top-of-atmosphere radiation combined with ERA5 atmospheric energy divergence and storage over the ocean. The annual time series correlate at 0.88, and the global energy budget is closed within ±0.5Wm −2 on interannual time scales. This unprecedented level of precision in the closure paves the way for detecting and tracking, within the energy budget, the excess energy entering the system due to the positive, time-averaged EEI of ~1 W.m −2. This closure also confirms the robustness of the observed 0.47±0.4Wm −2 dec −1 increase in Earth’s energy imbalance by CERES and demonstrates that the vast majority of excess energy is stored in the ocean including the excess energy coming from the radiative imbalance over land.

item.title: Fidelity and stratigraphy of the Antarctic Allan Hills old ice archive from continuous flow analysis
item.dc:creator: Abigail Hudak, Asmita Banerjee, Christo Buizert, Edward Brook, Michael Kalk, Lindsey Davidge, … (+13)
item.description:
Climate of the Past — matched: Antarctic, interglacial, ice core
The Allan Hills contains the oldest known ice, extending records millions of years. However, this area along the Transantarctic Mountains margin results in stratigraphically discontinuous ice core records. Here, we investigate high-resolution geochemical records to better constrain biases and stratigraphic complexities, and find these records exhibit reduced variance, some degree of interglacial bias, with varying behaviours across ice cores at the Allan Hills.

item.title: Structurally preconditioned continental-shelf troughs define potential warm-water pathways in Lützow-Holm Bay, East Antarctica
item.dc:creator: Masakazu Fujii, Yoshifumi Nogi
item.description:
Scientific Reports — matched: glacier, Antarctica, Holocene
We present new shipboard bathymetry from Lützow-Holm Bay, East Antarctica, acquired during three summers with reduced fast-ice cover to resolve glacier-front bathymetry and assess its relationship to inherited crustal structure and potential warm-water access. Echo-soundings in front of glacier systems reveal a network of deep troughs and shallow sills across the inner continental shelf. The Shirase Glacier system is connected to the deeper continental shelf through an entrance approximately 740 m deep, whereas shallower sills of approximately 480–580 m occur at the entrances to the Skallen, Telen, and Honnør glacier-front troughs. These depth contrasts define bathymetric thresholds that may modulate warm-water access under varying oceanographic conditions. The NW–SE-trending segment of the main trough is spatially aligned with a structural lineament inferred from a major airborne magnetic-anomaly boundary, suggesting that inherited basement structure may have influenced the localization of glacial erosion. Together, these observations suggest that inherited basement structure may have helped shape a segmented trough-and-sill morphology that now provides potential pathways and bathymetric thresholds for warm-water access, offering a geological framework for interpreting modern and Holocene ice–ocean interactions in Lützow-Holm Bay.

item.title: Three decades of in situ snow accumulation at Neumayer, coastal Antarctica: trends, variability, and recent extremes
item.dc:creator: Valerie Reppert, Olaf Eisen, Holger Schmithüsen, Stefanie Arndt, Guido Ascenso, Linda Ort, … (+1)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: Antarctica
We analyzed 33 years of snow accumulation measurements at Neumayer Station, Antarctica, to understand changes in the amount of snow building up on the surface over time. The long-term, high-resolution data show mostly stable accumulation, but rare positive extremes appeared in 2021 and 2023. Seasonal and multi-year patterns were identified, providing valuable data to improve climate models and satellite observations.

item.description:

item.title: Respecting the boundaries: balancing climate adaptation and Earth system resilience
item.dc:creator: Bastian Ott, Jonathan F. Donges, Johan Rockström
item.description:
Earth System Dynamics — matched: Earth system, greenhouse gas, climate change
Climate adaptation is crucial but its impacts on the Earth system are not well understood. Our study finds climate adaptation contributes ~26 % of annual greenhouse gas emissions, ~74 % of human freshwater withdrawals, and even affects the ozone layer. While some of these impacts are driven by climate change, the majority is likely fuelled by economic, demographic, and technological developments. These findings highlight the need to balance adaptation with respect for Earth system resilience.

item.title: Brief communication: The Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation is not a reliable indicator of the timing of an ice-free Arctic
item.dc:creator: Christopher Wyburn-Powell, Alexandra Jahn
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: Arctic, sea ice
The Arctic Ocean is expected to become seasonally ice-free within a few decades. Previous research using one climate model showed that a major climate pattern called the Interdecadal Pacific Oscillation (IPO) could narrow predictions of when this will happen. Using a broader selection of the latest climate models, we show the IPO is not a reliable predictor of ice-free timing. However, the IPO may still influence the rate and location of Arctic sea ice reduction over the next two decades.

item.title: Modulation of glacier surge cycles on decadal to centennial timescales by intrinsic thermal-structure variability
item.dc:creator: Andrew Nolan, Gwenn E. Flowers, Andy Aschwanden, Adrien Gilbert
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: glacier
We used a computer model to study the effects of glacier "surges", or unusual fast-flow events, on the distribution of ice temperature in a glacier. The purpose of the study was to examine feedbacks that might influence the form and flow of these glaciers in a stable climate. We found surging glaciers to be smaller and colder than their ordinary counterparts, while strong regular surges induced an oscillation in glacier temperature and flow speed much longer than the interval between surges.

item.title: Vanishing Glaciers, Emerging Crises: A Perception-Based Case Study of Water Scarcity in Ladakh
item.dc:creator: Zulfiqar Ali Beigh, Mansoor Ahmad Lone
item.category: Inventum Biologicum: An International Journal of Biological Research
item.description:
Inventum Biologicum: An International Journal of Biological Research — matched: glacier
Ladakh is a high-altitude cold desert whose agriculture, drinking water supply and ecosystems depend on glacier melt and seasonal snow. This study examines how local people perceive climatic and hydrological change, its socio-economic consequences, the role of tourism and urbanization, and the effectiveness of traditional and modern water management. A structured questionnaire was administered to 100 purposively selected respondents (40% farmers, 25% local residents, 20% tourism-related workers and 15% herders), and responses were analysed as percentages. Most respondents reported earlier glacier melting (80%), rising temperature (75%), reduced snowfall (68%) and a decline in drinking water availability (74%). Reduced irrigation (82%), falling income (75%), dependence on external food supply (75%) and food insecurity (73%) were widely reported. About 80% linked tourism and urbanization to rising water demand. Traditional systems (zings and kuhls) were well known (85%) and judged environmentally suitable (82%), yet 68% reported declining use. Ice Stupas were considered suitable for Ladakh by 85%, and 88% supported integrating traditional and modern methods. The findings are perception-based and drawn from a non-probability sample, but they point to a combined climatic and anthropogenic water crisis and support a participatory framework that integrates indigenous knowledge, modern technology and stronger regulation.

item.title: Snowmelt influence on Northern Hemisphere river discharge – the potential of causal inference for assessing long-term trends
item.dc:creator: Samuel Schilling, Tobias Bolch, Andreas Dietz, Rebecca Jean Herman, Claudia Kuenzer
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: snowpack
Snow stored in winter snowpacks supplies water to rivers that millions depend on. As warming reduces snow amounts, we studied whether melting snow still matters for river flow. Using long records from basins on four continents and cause-and-effect analysis, we found that in some basins, snowmelt's causal role in river flow is growing, even as both the snowpack and the river flow itself decline.

item.title: Kinetic partitioning with effective mass accommodation for secondary organic aerosol simulations in chemical transport modeling
item.dc:creator: Regina Luu, Meredith Schervish, Samuel E. O'Donnell, Jeffrey R. Pierce, Manabu Shiraiwa
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
The occurrence of semisolid and glassy phase states in SOA (Secondary organic aerosols) challenges traditional model treatments of equilibrium partitioning of SOA. We developed an effective method to treat kinetic partitioning of SOA by resolving the effects of particle phase state in chemical transport modeling. The application in GEOS-Chem (Goddard Earth Observing System - Chemistry) reveals that SOA budget is impacted significantly especially over drylands and in the upper troposphere.
